l: temptation, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: is common to man Temptation is said to be common to man, and God will not allow believers to be tempted above what they are able. He will provide a way of escape so they can endure it. The fathers' lusting is given as an example of yielding to evil desires.

l: Lord's Supper, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The Lord's Supper is the bread and cup that Paul received from the Lord Jesus, instituted on the night he was betrayed. The cup and bread share in Christ's blood and body, making the many one body and excluding demons' table. Paul rebukes the Corinthians' selfish meal as not the Lord's supper, presenting it as a memorial proclaiming his death until he comes, and warns against unworthy eating.

l: man, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Man is portrayed as head of woman, with Christ as his head, and as God's image and glory. He should not cover his head when praying or prophesying, yet he is not independent of woman, coming through birth.

l: woman, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Woman is portrayed in relation to man: his glory, drawn from him and made for him, yet not independent of him in the Lord. She is told to cover her head when praying or prophesying, holds authority over her head because of the angels, and has long hair as a glory and covering.

l: head covering, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: A head covering is required of a woman who prays or prophesies and forbidden to a man doing the same. Paul supports this with arguments from headship, creation, the angels, nature, and the practice of God's assemblies, and treats it as a matter of honor and shame.

l: spiritual gifts, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Spiritual gifts are varied manifestations of the one Spirit, given to each person for the profit of all. Listed kinds include the word of wisdom, word of knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, languages and interpretation of languages. Chapter 12 explains that not all have the same gifts and urges earnest desire for the best, with a more excellent way to come. Chapter 14 stresses desiring gifts, especially prophesying, to build up the assembly.

l: body (church as body of Christ), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The body is the church as the body of Christ: one body with many members, formed by baptism in one Spirit of Jews, Greeks, bond or free. God composed it without division, so members care for one another, suffering and rejoicing together.

l: members of the body, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The body is a community of individual believers, set by God in varied roles such as apostles, prophets and teachers. Each member has a place and needs the others; seemingly weaker or less honorable parts are necessary and receive more honor. With equal care and no division, all share in suffering and honor.

l: faith, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: remains permanently [one of three that remain] Faith is mentioned as being able to remove mountains, but the speaker says that having all such faith without love leaves him nothing. At the end it is listed with hope and love as one of three things that remain. It is ranked below love, which is the greatest.

l: speaking in other languages, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Speaking in another language is directed to God, edifying only the speaker unless interpreted. It is a sign for unbelievers, limited to two or three speakers in turn with an interpreter, silent without one, and not forbidden.

l: prophesying, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Prophesying speaks to men for edification, exhortation, and consolation, edifying the assembly. It surpasses uninterpreted speaking in languages and is a sign to believers. Two or three prophets speak in turn while others discern, so all may prophesy one by one, learn, and be exhorted.

l: wives, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Wives are instructed in Chapter 14 to stay quiet in the assemblies, speaking only in submission as the law says; if they wish to learn, they should ask their husbands at home, since speaking there is shameful.

l: order and peace in worship, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: A topic on order and peace in worship: because God is not a God of confusion but of peace, speaking is regulated. Tongue speakers take turns with an interpreter or silence, prophets speak singly while others discern, and all ends decently and in order.

l: Adam, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Adam is the first man, made of dust and earth, who became a living soul. Death came through him and all die in him; contrasted with Christ, the last Adam, a life-giving spirit, humans bear his earthly image.

l: resurrection of the dead, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Resurrection of the dead is a doctrine some among the Corinthians deny and Paul disputes. Its reality is bound to Christ's: without it, preaching, faith and the dead in Christ are vain. It came by man, as death did; Christ rises first, then his people at his coming, defended against objections.

l: death, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Death entered through man, and in Adam all die. Its sting is sin, empowered by the law. It is the last enemy abolished, swallowed up in victory when the perishable becomes imperishable.

l: resurrection body, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The resurrection body is described in Chapter 15 as sown perishable, in dishonor and weakness, a natural body, then raised imperishable, in glory and power, a spiritual body. Illustrated by a dying seed and differing celestial and terrestrial glories, it requires perishable and mortal to put on imperishability and immortality; believers bear the heavenly image.

l: collection for the saints, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: A gracious gift collected for the saints, commanded by Paul to the Corinthians as to the Galatian assemblies. Each person saves on the first day of every week as he prospers, avoiding collections on Paul's arrival; approved messengers then carry it with letters to Jerusalem.

This document is Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians, thirteen chapters in which Paul, with Timothy and co-workers, writes to the assembly at Corinth and the saints in Achaia. The most important figures are Paul, the Corinthian believers, Titus, and Christ, with God as the source of comfort and power. It opens by blessing God, who comforts Paul in affliction so he can comfort others, and Paul defends his changed travel plans, insisting God's promises are 'Yes' in Christ. Chapters 2 and 7 deal with a painful earlier letter, a person who caused sorrow and should now be forgiven, and Paul's anxiety at Troas until Titus arrived in Macedonia with good news; Paul distinguishes godly sorrow leading to repentance from worldly sorrow. Chapters 3 to 5 reflect on the ministry itself: the Corinthians are Christ's living letter, the new covenant of the Spirit surpasses the glory of Moses' covenant, the ministers carry treasure in clay vessels, and the earthly tent contrasts with an eternal house. All will face Christ's judgment seat, and believers are new creations given the ministry of reconciliation as ambassadors for Christ. Chapter 6 urges the Corinthians to receive grace now, lists the ministers' hardships and paradoxes, asks them to open their hearts, and warns against being unequally yoked with unbelievers. Chapters 8 and 9 turn to the collection for the saints, holding up the generous but poor Macedonians and Christ's own becoming poor as examples, sending Titus and two brothers, and teaching that God loves a cheerful giver and that giving produces thanksgiving. Chapters 10 to 13 form a defense of Paul's apostolic authority against critics and self-commending rivals he calls false apostles. He boasts reluctantly, listing his labors, sufferings, and his escape from Damascus in a basket, and describes being caught up to the third heaven. He recounts his thorn in the flesh, to which the Lord answered that grace is sufficient and power is perfected in weakness. He announces a third visit, fears finding strife and unrepented sin, and warns he will not spare offenders. He urges the Corinthians to test themselves, closing with calls to rejoice, be of one mind, live in peace, greetings from the saints, and a benediction naming the Lord Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit.

Paul is an apostle of Christ Jesus by God's will, writing with Timothy to the assembly of God at Corinth. The records present him as a pastor defending his sincerity, authority and conduct to a community in which critics call him lowly in presence, bold only when absent, weak in body and unskilled in speech. Most important is his relationship with the Corinthians: he loves them, bears anxiety for all the assemblies, feels godly jealousy for them as a bride promised to one husband, Christ, and calls himself a fellow worker who works for their joy rather than controlling their faith. He trusts in God who raises the dead and hopes to be delivered still. He boasts of a clear conscience, of the Corinthians mutually, and of Achaia's readiness to Macedonia. He claims his word in letters matches his deed in person, and he takes approval from the Lord, not self-commendation. The account unfolds from the opening, where Paul describes comfort in affliction, despair of life in Asia, his changed travel plans, and his sparing the Corinthians by not coming. He writes in sorrow and tears, urges forgiveness of an offender, and is relieved in Macedonia when Titus arrives with good news of their repentance, so he no longer regrets his letter. He then turns to the collection for the saints, sending Titus and brothers, avoiding blame in administering it, and urging cheerful, bountiful giving. Next he defends his authority against critics: he walks in the flesh but does not war by it, keeps within the sphere God appointed reaching to Corinth, and hopes to preach beyond. He asserts that he is not inferior to the best apostles, a Hebrew, Israelite and offspring of Abraham, and a servant of Christ more than his rivals, recounting hardships and his escape from Damascus in a basket. Reluctantly boasting, he speaks of a man caught up to Paradise and a thorn in the flesh, glorying in weakness so Christ's power rests on him. He performed signs and wonders, was no financial burden, and will spend and be spent for their souls. He ends by fearing strife and disorder on his coming third visit, mourning those who have not repented, warning he will not spare them, exhorting, blessing, and noting his authority is for building up, not tearing down.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, 2 Corinthians
s: The assembly of God at Corinth is a community of believers located in Corinth, addressed by Paul and Timothy together with all the saints in Achaia. The records portray a congregation that stands firm in faith, shares in Paul's afflictions, sufferings and comfort, and helps him through supplication. Paul treats them as his boast, as he is theirs. Early on, they are shown as strong: they abound in faith, utterance, knowledge, earnestness and love, and they were first to start the grace of giving, the collection for the saints, a year earlier. They are urged to complete it according to what they have and to show proof of their love to the sent brothers before the assemblies. Their relationship with Paul is marked by repentance and reconciliation. Grieved by his letter, they showed earnest care, zeal and vindication, refreshed Titus's spirit, and received him with fear and trembling, leaving Paul confident about them. Concerns also emerge. Paul hopes their faith grows and their obedience is made full, so he need not show boldness when present. He reminds them they were promised to Christ as a pure virgin, fears their minds being deceived, and rebukes them for tolerating preachers of another Jesus, spirit or good news. He notes that the signs of an apostle were worked among them, that he seeks them and not their possessions, and that he fears strife, jealousy and factions. The account ends with warnings that Paul will not spare those who sinned, a call to test themselves whether they are in the faith, and exhortations to rejoice, be perfected, be of the same mind and live in peace, with greetings from all the saints.

God is presented across these records as the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, and the God of love and peace. The most important thing about him is his role as comforter, deliverer, and reconciler. He comforts in all affliction and comforts the lowly, as when he comforted Paul through the coming of Titus. He is faithful, raises the dead, and delivered Paul from so great a death and still does. He holds the promises and raised Jesus Christ, and he will raise Paul and his fellow ministers through Jesus and present the Corinthian believers together with them. The account begins in Chapter 1 with his titles, his comfort, and his faithfulness. He establishes and anoints Paul and his companions, and he gives the Holy Spirit as a down payment in their hearts. In the next chapters he leads Paul in triumph in Christ, makes the ministers sufficient as servants of a new covenant, and, as the living God, writes on hearts by his Spirit. He has shone in the ministers' hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ. He is the source of the exceeding greatness of power. Chapter 5 is central. God made the ministers for being clothed with life and gave the Spirit as a down payment. He reconciles the world in Christ, not reckoning trespasses, and reconciles Paul and his fellow ministers through Jesus Christ. He entrusted the word of reconciliation to the ministers. He made Christ to be sin on our behalf so that we become the righteousness of God in him. In Chapter 6 he promises to dwell among his people, be their God, and be a Father to them as sons and daughters, and he is called the Lord Almighty. The later chapters turn to giving. He puts earnest care for the Corinthians into Titus and is credited with the grace given in the Macedonian assemblies. He loves a cheerful giver and is able to make all grace abound to Achaia. He supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, multiplies the seed, and increases the fruits of righteousness. Thanksgiving and glory go to him for these gifts. Chapter 11 calls him the blessed God and Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, who knows Paul does not lie. At the close, his power is the source by which Christ lives and by which Paul and his companions will live with him. He is the God of love and peace, and his love is named in the closing benediction.

Christ, called Jesus Christ, is presented across Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians as the Son of God, the image of God, and the Lord preached by the apostles. The letter opens with him as the "Yes" to all God's promises, the one through whom comes the "Amen" to God's glory, and the source of comfort that abounds as his sufferings abound to Paul and his companions. Through the middle chapters he is the one in whose presence Paul forgives, in whom God leads the ministers in triumph, and whose letter the Corinthian believers are shown to be. In him the veil over the old covenant passes away. The letter then centers on his death and resurrection: he died for all so that the living might live for him, he knew no sin yet was made sin on our behalf, and God was in him reconciling the world. He holds the judgment seat before which all must be revealed. His putting to death is carried in the ministers' bodies so that his life may be revealed. He has no agreement with Belial, which grounds the call not to be yoked with unbelievers. He is the model of grace, becoming poor though rich for the Corinthians' sakes. His humility and gentleness ground Paul's entreaty, and every thought is to be taken captive to obedience to him. Paul promises the Corinthians to him as one husband and warns against false apostles who masquerade as his. The portrait closes with him crucified through weakness yet living through God's power, present in the believers unless they are disqualified, and with the benediction invoking his grace.

The Spirit of the living God is identified with the Lord. He writes the Corinthians as a letter on hearts, gives life in contrast to the killing letter, grants liberty, transforms believers from glory to glory, and his service has greater glory.
Achaia, a place, was reportedly prepared for a year, its zeal inspiring many Macedonians; Paul, fearing it might be unprepared if Macedonians arrive, sends the brothers to ready its promised gift.
Paul has boasted to those of Macedonia about Achaia's readiness, and Achaia's zeal stirred up very many of them. Paul notes that some from Macedonia may come with him and find Achaia unprepared.

Comfort is a central theme in Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians. It comes from God, who comforts Paul in affliction so he can comfort others, and it abounds through Christ. In Chapter 1 it brings the Corinthians patient endurance and steadfast hope; in Chapter 7 it overflows as joy through Titus's coming and his refreshed spirit.

purpose comfort and salvation of the Corinthians [Paul's affliction] Paul says the sufferings of Christ abound to him and that his afflictions serve the Corinthians' comfort and salvation. The Corinthians are partakers of the same sufferings and endure them patiently. These afflictions come with God's comfort.

In Asia, Paul and his companions were weighed down exceedingly, beyond their power, despairing of life and feeling sentenced to death. This taught them to trust in God who raises the dead, not themselves. God delivered them, and Paul hopes for further deliverance.

Paul's planned itinerary: visit Corinth first, go on to Macedonia, return to Corinth, then be sent by the Corinthians to Judea. He changed the plan and did not come to Corinth, saying this was to spare them. He denies fickleness or fleshly planning, insisting his word was not 'Yes and no.'

Boasting is a recurring theme in which Paul argues its proper object is the Lord and, if he must boast, it concerns weakness. In Chapter 10 he refuses to boast beyond his God-appointed limits or in others' labors, holding that the Lord's commendation matters. In Chapter 11 he boasts reluctantly, as foolishness, since many boast after the flesh, compares credentials and sufferings with rivals, and resolves to boast of weakness, citing the Damascus basket escape. In Chapter 12 he calls it unprofitable, says the Corinthians compelled him, and boasts only of weaknesses and the man caught up to Paradise.

Corinthians is a community of believers addressed by Paul and his co-workers, portrayed as both recipients of instruction and a living testimony. Early on, they are described as a letter of Christ, written in the ministers' hearts, known and read by all, inscribed by the Spirit of the living God on hearts of flesh rather than with ink on stone, and serving as the ministers' commendation. They are told to forgive and comfort an offender already sufficiently punished, with their obedience proving their commitment. The ministers serve for their sake, with life working in the believers and thanksgiving abounding through grace. Finally, they are urged not to receive God's grace in vain, told they are restricted by their own affections rather than the apostles, asked to open their hearts, warned against unequal yoking with unbelievers, and identified as a temple of the living God, called to separate.

l: offender (the one who caused sorrow), 2 Corinthians
s: He is described as having caused sorrow not chiefly to Paul but in part to all of the recipients. He has received a punishment inflicted by the many, which is declared sufficient, and Paul asks that he be forgiven and comforted lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

Titus is a partner and fellow worker of Paul for the Corinthians. His coming comforted Paul and his companions in Macedonia, as he reported the Corinthians' longing, mourning, and zeal. His spirit was refreshed by them, and Paul's boasts about them proved true. His affection for them grows as he remembers their obedience. Urged to complete the giving he had begun among them, he went to them earnestly of his own accord, walking in Paul's spirit.

l: sorrow (grief caused by Paul's earlier letter), 2 Corinthians
s: Paul says he would not come again in sorrow, and that his letter was written not to make the recipients grieve but so they would know his love. He notes that whoever caused sorrow did so in part to them all, and that the offender risks being swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

Paul urges the recipients to forgive the offender, comfort him, and confirm their love toward him. He states that he forgives whomever they forgive, doing so for their sakes in Christ's presence, so that Satan gains no advantage over them.

The Good News of Christ is the message of Christ's glory as God's image; it stays veiled to the dying, whose minds the god of this world blinded, while ministers commend themselves by truth, not deceit.

Moses is a figure whose face shone with fading glory so intensely that the Israelites could not look steadily at it. He wore a veil so they would not see the glory's end, and to this day a veil lies on the hearts of those hearing Moses read.

has_state hardened minds The children of Israel could not look steadily at Moses' face because of its glory. Moses veiled his face so they would not see the end of the passing glory. Their minds were hardened, and a veil remains over their hearts when Moses is read.

l: Paul and his fellow ministers (we), 2 Corinthians
s: The entity is Paul and his fellow ministers, a group of apostolic servants who write to the Corinthian believers and describe who they are and what they do. They say they need no letters of commendation, since the Corinthians themselves are the letter of Christ. Their confidence and sufficiency come from God, not themselves, and God has made them servants of a new covenant. Most important is their ministry of reconciliation: God gave them the word of reconciliation, and they act as ambassadors for Christ, urging people to be reconciled to God. They preach Jesus Christ as Lord, not themselves, and serve the Corinthians for Jesus' sake. The account unfolds in four movements. First, they speak boldly with unveiled faces, being transformed into the Lord's image from glory to glory by the Spirit. Second, having received mercy, they do not faint and renounce shameful hidden things. They hold treasure in clay vessels, so the power is God's, and though the outward person decays, the inward is renewed daily. Third, they groan in the earthly tent, long for the heavenly habitation, and walk by faith rather than sight, aiming to please Christ and driven by his love. Finally, they commend themselves as God's servants through hardships, beatings, imprisonments, and labors, yet are always rejoicing, poor yet making many rich. They close by declaring an open mouth and enlarged heart toward the Corinthians, speaking as to children and asking for the same openness in return.
The new covenant is of the Spirit, not the letter; God made its servants sufficient. Its service of righteousness exceeds the earlier service in glory, and it remains and gives life.
The old covenant is a service of death and condemnation, engraved on stone tablets, whose letter kills. It came with fading glory, and a veil still remains over its reading, removed only in Christ.

The veil is an object first placed on Moses' face to keep Israel from seeing the fading glory's end. It stays over hearts during the reading of the old covenant, but is removed in Christ whenever someone turns to the Lord, leaving believers unveiled.

Glory marked the service of death and condemnation, seen in Moses' face, but that glory was passing away. The service of the Spirit and of righteousness has much more glory and remains. Believers who see the Lord's glory as in a mirror are transformed into his image from glory to glory.

has_purpose show power is of God The ministers say they have this treasure in clay vessels, meaning the light of the knowledge of God's glory in their hearts held in frail bodies. This is so that the exceeding greatness of the power may be seen to be of God and not from themselves.

is light and momentary [produces an eternal weight of glory] The ministers are pressed on every side, perplexed, pursued and struck down, yet not crushed, driven to despair, forsaken or destroyed. They are always delivered to death for Jesus' sake so that his life is revealed in them. Their light affliction, lasting only a moment, works for them an eternal weight of glory far beyond it.
Our earthly tent, the mortal body, may be dissolved, leaving us groaning and burdened; the hope is to be clothed so life swallows mortality, though at home in the body we are absent from the Lord.
An eternal house not made with hands, a building from God in the heavens; we groan longing to be clothed with it, and we have it once the earthly tent is dissolved.
Christ's judgment seat is where all must be revealed and each receives recompense for deeds done in the body, good or bad; knowing this, ministers persuade people in the fear of the Lord.
New creation is the state of anyone in Christ: old things pass away and all things become new, linked to no longer knowing anyone according to the flesh.

originates_from God Reconciliation is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ and gave the ministry and word of reconciliation to the ministers. God was in Christ reconciling the world, not reckoning trespasses to them. The ministers, as ambassadors, plead with people to be reconciled to God.

l: grace of giving (collection for the saints), 2 Corinthians
s: The grace of giving is a collection serving the saints. In Chapter 8, the Macedonians plead to share in it and Titus is to complete it; it is acceptable according to what one has and administered honorably before the Lord and men. In Chapter 9, the Achaians' earlier promise is to be prepared ahead as generosity, given willingly as decided in the heart. It aims at equality, supplies lack, and produces much thanksgiving to God.

is_time now The day of salvation is drawn from a quoted saying about an acceptable time when God listened and helped. The text declares that now is the acceptable time and now is the day of salvation, which gives urgency to the plea not to receive God's grace in vain.

l: hardships and sufferings of the apostles' ministry, 2 Corinthians
s: The ministry's sufferings are listed as great endurance, afflictions, hardships, distresses, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, watchings, and fastings. They are part of how the apostles commend themselves as servants of God, alongside glory and dishonor, evil and good report, and being punished yet not killed. They are paired with paradoxes of sorrow yet rejoicing and poverty yet making many rich.

has_no_fellowship_with believer [believers should not be unequally yoked] Unbelievers are those with whom the Corinthians are told not to be unequally yoked. The text asks what fellowship, agreement, or portion righteousness, light, Christ, and a believer can have with iniquity, darkness, Belial, and an unbeliever. The call to come out from among them and touch no unclean thing follows.

l: temple of the living God, 2 Corinthians
s: The Corinthians are identified as a temple of the living God, incompatible with idols; God promises to dwell and walk in them, being their God and they his people.

l: letter (Paul's letter to the Corinthians), 2 Corinthians
s: The letter grieved the recipients, though only for a while, and the author regretted sending it before ceasing to regret it. It led them to repentance. He says he wrote it neither for the sake of the one who did wrong nor the one who suffered wrong, but so that the recipients' earnest care for him would be revealed before God.

produces repentance [leads to salvation, brings no regret] Godly sorrow is said to produce repentance leading to salvation, which brings no regret, in contrast to the sorrow of the world, which produces death. The recipients were grieved in a godly way and so suffered no loss through the author. It worked in them earnest care, defense, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, and vindication.

The assemblies of Macedonia, enduring severe affliction and deep poverty, nonetheless gave with abundant joy, willingly and beyond their means. They begged to share in the collection for the saints, having first given themselves to the Lord and to the writer's party.

The saints are recipients of the giving service that supplies their lack; they glorify God for Achaia's obedience and generosity, and with supplication yearn for them because of God's exceeding grace in them.

is_illustrated_by Scripture (quoted about manna) [he who gathered much had nothing left over] Equality is the stated purpose of the giving: not that others be eased and the addressees distressed. Their present abundance supplies others' lack so that others' abundance may later supply theirs, as with the gathered manna where he who gathered much had nothing left over and he who gathered little had no lack.

has_role arrange the generous gift ahead of time [go before to Achaia] Paul has sent the brothers, entreating them to go ahead to Achaia and arrange the promised generous gift beforehand. Their purpose is that Paul's boasting not be in vain and that the gift be ready as generosity, not greediness.

says_to_paul grace is sufficient [power is made perfect in weakness] The Lord is the source of the visions and revelations Paul mentions. When Paul begged him three times about the thorn, he replied that his grace is sufficient and that his power is made perfect in weakness.

l: critics (those who consider Paul to walk according to the flesh), 2 Corinthians
s: These critics consider Paul and his companions to be walking according to the flesh, and they say his letters are weighty and strong but his bodily presence is weak and his speech despised. Paul tells such a person to consider that he is in deed when present what he is in word by letters when absent. He also tells them he is ready to avenge disobedience once the Corinthians' obedience is full.

l: self-commending rivals (those who commend themselves), 2 Corinthians
s: These people commend themselves, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, and Paul says they are without understanding. Paul declines to number or compare himself with them. Their way of boasting is contrasted with approval that comes from the Lord's commendation.

Paul says that though he walks in the flesh, he does not wage war according to the flesh. The weapons of this warfare are mighty before God for throwing down strongholds, imaginations and every high thing exalted against the knowledge of God, and for bringing every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.

Paul's apostolic authority is given by the Lord to build up the Corinthians, not tear them down. He will boast of it without shame, denies intending to terrify by letters, affirms it is the same in presence and writing, and notes God-appointed limits reaching Corinth.

False apostles are deceitful workers who masquerade as Christ's apostles, like Satan posing as an angel of light, serving him as false servants of righteousness. Paul acts against their claims to equality with him; their end matches their works.

Paul's sufferings are listed in Chapter 11 as labors, prisons, excessive stripes and frequent deaths: five Jewish floggings, three rod beatings, a stoning, three shipwrecks, a night and day in the deep, many perils, deprivations, and daily anxiety for all the assemblies.

Paul's free preaching of God's Good News to the Corinthians, humbling himself so they might be exalted. He accepted support from other assemblies and Macedonian brothers so he burdened no one, and vows to continue this in Achaia, denying boasters any opportunity.

l: man in Christ (caught up into Paradise), 2 Corinthians
s: A man in Christ, known to Paul, was caught up fourteen years earlier into the third heaven, Paradise, uncertain whether in or out of the body. He heard unspeakable words not lawful to utter; Paul will boast on his behalf.

The thorn in the flesh is a messenger of Satan sent to torment Paul, given to keep him from excessive exaltation after great revelations. Paul pleaded three times for its removal; it stayed, and he was told grace suffices.

Paul says he comes to visions and revelations of the Lord, illustrated by the man caught up to the third heaven and Paradise. Their exceeding greatness is given as the reason a thorn in the flesh was given to keep Paul from being exalted excessively.

Paul says he will boast in his weaknesses and glory in them so that the power of Christ may rest on him. He takes pleasure in weaknesses, injuries, necessities, persecutions and distresses for Christ's sake, concluding that when he is weak, then he is strong.

Paul says the Corinthians were not made inferior to other assemblies except that he was not a burden to them, and he asks forgiveness for this wrong. He affirms he will not burden them, since parents should save up for children, and he denies taking advantage of them himself or through Titus and the brother he sent.

Paul announces his third visit to the Corinthians, saying he is ready to come and will not burden them. He fears finding them unprepared and being humbled by God as he mourns those who sinned. He warned them on his second visit and now writes while absent, so that if he comes again he will not spare sinners, using his authority to build up.

include uncleanness, sexual immorality, lustfulness [unrepented by many] Paul fears he may find strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, factions, slander, whisperings, proud thoughts and riots among the Corinthians. He also expects to mourn for many who have sinned and not repented of uncleanness, sexual immorality and lustfulness.

has_subject_matter whether Jesus Christ is in the readers Paul commands the Corinthians to examine and test themselves to see whether they are in the faith, asking whether they do not know that Jesus Christ is in them, unless they are disqualified. He answers their demand for proof of Christ speaking in him by turning the test back on them, and he hopes they will know that he and his companions are not disqualified.

This document is Paul's Letter to the Galatians, a six-chapter epistle written by Paul, an apostle commissioned through Jesus Christ and God the Father, together with the brothers with him, to the assemblies of Galatia. Its central concern is that the Galatians are deserting the true Good News for a different, perverted gospel that insists on circumcision and works of the law. The most important figures are Paul, the Galatians, Christ, Abraham, and the Jerusalem leaders (Peter/Cephas, James, John), with Barnabas and Titus in supporting roles. Chapter 1 opens with greeting, astonishment at the Galatians' quick defection, and a curse on anyone preaching a different gospel. Paul insists his message came by revelation of Jesus Christ, and recounts his former persecution of the assembly, his call, his time in Arabia, Damascus, Jerusalem, Syria and Cilicia. Chapter 2 describes his Jerusalem visit after fourteen years, where Titus was not compelled to be circumcised and James, Cephas, and John extended fellowship, agreeing Paul and Barnabas would go to the Gentiles. He then recounts opposing Peter at Antioch for withdrawing from Gentiles, and argues that people are justified by faith in Christ, not works of the law, and that Christ lives in him. Chapter 3 rebukes the Galatians as foolish, appeals to Abraham's faith, and argues that Christ redeemed believers from the law's curse, that the promise to Abraham and his offspring, Christ, is not annulled by the later law, which served as a tutor until faith came; all in Christ are one, children of God and heirs. Chapter 4 uses the image of an heir under guardians, God sending his Son so believers receive adoption and the Spirit crying 'Abba, Father,' rebukes the return to elemental principles and observed days, and gives an allegory of Hagar and the free woman representing two covenants, concluding the readers are children of promise. Chapter 5 urges standing firm in Christ's liberty, warns that circumcision obligates one to the whole law, says love fulfills the law, and contrasts the deeds of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit. Chapter 6 gives instructions for community life: restoring the faulty gently, bearing burdens, supporting teachers, and sowing to the Spirit rather than the flesh. Writing in large letters, Paul accuses those compelling circumcision of avoiding persecution, boasts only in the cross, declares a new creation matters, mentions bearing Jesus's marks, and closes with a blessing and prayer for grace.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Paul is the author of the letter to the Galatians, presenting himself as an apostle commissioned not by men but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, writing with the brothers who are with him. He calls himself a servant of Christ, not a pleaser of men. The records trace his life: he once persecuted the assembly of God beyond measure and advanced in the Jews' religion beyond many his age, but God separated him from his mother's womb and called him by grace, revealing the Son in him so he would preach to the Gentiles. After time in Arabia and Damascus, he visited Peter for fifteen days after three years, then went to Syria and Cilicia. Fourteen years later he went to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, laid his Good News before the leaders, refused the false brothers, and received the right hand of fellowship from James, Cephas and John, recognized as entrusted with the gospel for the uncircumcised. He resisted Peter at Antioch. Central to his stance is that he died to the law to live to God, was crucified with Christ, lives by faith in the Son of God, and does not reject God's grace. Toward the Galatians he is anxious: he first preached to them in bodily weakness, fears his labor was wasted, and is in travail until Christ is formed in them. He warns that circumcision profits nothing, notes he is still persecuted because he does not preach it, and urges them to walk by the Spirit rather than the flesh.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Jesus Christ, called Lord, is the central figure of Paul's Letter to the Galatians. He was raised from the dead by God the Father and gave himself for sins to deliver people from this present evil age, according to God's will. Paul received the Good News through a revelation of him and became an apostle through him. Paul says Christ lives in him and loves him. Christ is the singular offspring of Abraham's promise. He redeemed believers from the law's curse by becoming a curse for them, and he makes them free. Righteousness through the law would make his death pointless; those seeking justification by the law are alienated from him, and circumcision profits nothing. The letter shows him crucified among the Galatians, then closes with his cross as the sole ground of boasting, his marks borne on the author's body, and a prayer for his grace to be with the brothers' spirit.

l: God the Father, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: raised Jesus Christ [from the dead] God the Father, together with Jesus Christ, commissioned Paul as an apostle and raised Jesus from the dead; grace and peace come from him. He is the one to whom glory is due forever, and it was his good pleasure to separate Paul from his mother's womb, call him through grace, and reveal his Son in him so Paul might preach among the Gentiles.

l: Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The Galatians are the recipients of Paul's letter, addressed as the assemblies located in Galatia. They were called in Christ's grace and once served false gods before being known by God. The records trace a movement from rebuke to reassurance to exhortation. In Chapter 1 they are greeted, then rebuked for quickly deserting the one who called them for a different 'good news', troubled by some who would pervert the gospel. In Chapter 3 they are called foolish and asked whether they received the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith. They are told they are children of God through faith, baptized into Christ and having put him on, and, as Christ's, Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise. In Chapter 4 they are sons and heirs, adopted through Christ's redemption and no longer bondservants, yet rebuked for turning back to elemental principles and observing days, months, seasons, and years, though they once welcomed Paul as an angel of God. They are children of promise, like the free woman's son, not of the servant. In Chapter 5 they are urged to stand firm in liberty, avoid a yoke of bondage, serve one another in love, and walk by the Spirit, since they were running well until interfered with and Paul is confident of them.

l: Good News of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The Good News of Christ is the gospel Paul preached and the Galatians received, which he insists is the only one and not according to man. Chapter 1 stresses its divine origin and curses any different gospel. Chapter 2 shows Paul entrusted with it for the uncircumcised, affirmed by Jerusalem leaders, defended against false brothers, and violated by Peter's conduct.

l: different good news (false gospel), Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: A supposed 'good news' the Galatians are turning to, which Paul says is not truly another gospel. He declares that anyone preaching anything other than what was received, even an angel from heaven, is to be cursed.

l: troublers (those perverting the gospel), Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: want_to_pervert Good News of Christ [trouble the Galatians] The troublers are some people who trouble the Galatians and want to pervert the Good News of Christ. The text does not name them, but Paul says that anyone who preaches a different "good news" than the one received is to be cursed.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Paul preaches the Good News among the Gentiles, and James, Cephas, and John agreed that he and Barnabas should go to them. Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised. At Antioch Peter ate with Gentiles until he withdrew, and Paul asked why Peter compelled the Gentiles to live as Jews.

l: Peter, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Peter, called Cephas and reputed a pillar with James and John, is entrusted with the Good News for the circumcised. At Antioch he withdrew from eating with Gentiles, fearing the circumcised, and Paul opposed him, saying he stood condemned.

l: Paul's revelation, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: is_source_of Good News of Christ [Paul received it through revelation of Jesus Christ, not from man] Paul states that the Good News he preaches came to him through a revelation of Jesus Christ, not from man and not by being taught. God was pleased to reveal his Son in Paul so that he might preach him among the Gentiles, and Paul did not immediately confer with flesh and blood or go up to Jerusalem, but went into Arabia and returned to Damascus.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: God is presented as a single, impartial deity who shows no partiality to man and cannot be mocked. He worked through Peter among the circumcised and Paul among the Gentiles. He justifies Gentiles by faith, supplies the Spirit, and confirmed his covenant with Abraham, granting the inheritance by promise. When the fullness of time came, he sent his Son, born under the law, to redeem those under it, then sent the Spirit of his Son into believers' hearts, making them sons and heirs. The records close with moral accountability: whatever a man sows he reaps, and peace and mercy rest on God's Israel.

l: Jews, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Paul says that he and Peter are Jews by nature and not Gentile sinners, yet they believed in Christ Jesus to be justified by faith and not by works of the law. At Antioch the rest of the Jews joined Peter in his hypocrisy. Paul accuses Peter of living as the Gentiles do while compelling Gentiles to live as the Jews do.

l: circumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Circumcision is treated as worthless in Christ Jesus. In Chapter 5, receiving it makes Christ profit nothing and obligates a man to the whole law, and Paul's refusal to preach it explains the cross's offense. In Chapter 6, others press it for self-serving reasons, though even the circumcised do not keep the law.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The law is a recurring subject in these records, presented as unable to justify anyone: no flesh is justified by its works, but a man is justified through faith in Jesus Christ. In Chapter 2, Paul says he died to the law to live to God, and that righteousness through it would make Christ's death pointless. Chapter 4 says the Son was born under it to redeem others, and that it records Abraham's two sons, read as allegory. Chapter 5 warns that circumcision makes one a debtor to keep all of it and that seeking justification by it means falling from grace. The whole law is fulfilled in loving one's neighbor; those led by the Spirit are not under it, and no law opposes the fruit of the Spirit.

l: justification by faith, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: is_through Jesus Christ [not by works of the law] Paul states that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, and that even he and Peter believed in Christ to be justified by faith. He denies that seeking justification in Christ makes Christ a servant of sin. He says that if righteousness were through the law, Christ died for nothing.

l: Peter's hypocrisy at Antioch, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: At Antioch, Peter ate with Gentiles until people from James came, then withdrew out of fear of the circumcision party. Other Jews and Barnabas followed his hypocrisy, so Paul publicly rebuked Peter for straying from the Good News's truth.

l: Abraham, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Abraham is a man of faith who believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. Scripture foretold all nations blessed in him; his father-of-faith legacy extends to believers as children. He has son Isaac, born by promise, and received the inheritance by promise.

l: Spirit, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The Spirit is received by hearing of faith, not works of the law, and opposes the flesh. Through the Spirit believers await righteousness; those led by it are free from the law, bear its fruit, and are told to walk by it.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The law, as described in Chapter 3, places those relying on its works under a curse, is not of faith, and justifies no one before God. It arrived 430 years after the covenant without annulling the promise to Abraham, was added because of transgressions until the offspring came, was ordained through angels by a mediator, and served as a tutor leading people to Christ.

l: faith, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: makes_children_of Abraham [those who are of faith] Faith is the means by which the Galatians received the Spirit and by which the righteous live. Those who are of faith are children of Abraham, are justified, and receive the promise of the Spirit; faith has now come, so believers are no longer under a tutor.

l: promise (to Abraham), Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: was_spoken_to Abraham [and to his offspring] The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring, who is Christ, and the inheritance rests on promise rather than law. The law that came later does not annul it, and it is given by faith in Jesus Christ to those who believe, making believers heirs according to promise.

l: Son of God (Christ Jesus), Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Son of God, Christ Jesus, was sent by God, born to a woman and under the law, to redeem those under the law and bring adoption as children; readers received him as an angel, and the author labors until Christ is formed in them.

l: Isaac, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Isaac is presented as a model for readers: born through promise and according to the Spirit, son of the free woman, persecuted by the one born according to the flesh, and the one who will inherit.

l: Hagar, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Hagar, in the allegory, represents the covenant from Mount Sinai in Arabia, bearing children into bondage; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, enslaved together with her children.

l: free woman (Abraham's wife), Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The free woman bore Abraham's son through promise, in contrast to the servant's son born according to the flesh. The text quotes Scripture that the servant's son will not inherit with her son, and says the readers are children of the free woman, not of a servant.

l: Mount Sinai, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: is_located_in Arabia Mount Sinai is the source of one of the two covenants, which bears children to bondage. The text equates Hagar with Mount Sinai in Arabia.

l: Jerusalem that exists now, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The Jerusalem that exists now is said to be answered to by Hagar/Mount Sinai. It is in bondage with her children.

l: Jerusalem that is above, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The Jerusalem above is described as free and as the mother of us all, tied to the quoted promise that the barren and desolate will outnumber the married woman's children.

l: elemental principles of the world, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: is_a weak and miserable The elemental principles of the world are the things under which the author and readers were held in bondage when they were children. The readers are asked why they turn back to these weak and miserable principles and desire bondage to them again, as shown by observing days, months, seasons, and years.

l: adoption as children, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Adoption as children is the purpose for which the Son redeemed those under the law. Because the readers are children, God sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, so they are no longer bondservants but sons and heirs.

l: bondage, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Bondage describes the condition of a child heir under guardians, of the author and readers under the elemental principles, and of the readers before they knew God, when they served those who are not gods. It is also the condition of Hagar's children and the present Jerusalem, and the readers are warned against desiring it all over again.

l: two covenants, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: is_a allegory The two covenants are presented as an allegory of the two sons of Abraham. One is from Mount Sinai and bears children to bondage, which is Hagar, while the other corresponds to the free woman, the Jerusalem above, and the children of promise.

l: liberty, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Liberty is what Christ made believers free with, and they are told to stand firm in it. They were called for freedom but must not use it as an opportunity for the flesh; instead they use it to serve one another through love.

l: the flesh, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The flesh is a force that lusts against the Spirit and stands contrary to it; believers are warned not to fulfill its lust or use freedom for it, since those belonging to Christ have crucified it.

l: deeds of the flesh, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The deeds of the flesh are declared obvious and listed: sexual immorality, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, anger, envy, murders, drunkenness, orgies and similar. Paul warns that those practicing them will not inherit God's Kingdom.

l: fruit of the Spirit, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: includes love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control The fruit of the Spirit is listed as love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. The text says there is no law against such things.

l: cross of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: The cross of Christ, belonging to Jesus Christ the Lord, is the sole thing the author boasts in; through it the world and he are crucified to each other, unlike circumcision-compellers avoiding persecution.

l: those who compel circumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: A group accused of compelling circumcision: they seek a good impression in the flesh and avoid persecution for the cross of Christ, though circumcised themselves they do not keep the law, and they want recipients circumcised to boast in their flesh.

l: new creation, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: is what counts [in Christ Jesus] The new creation is named as what counts in Christ Jesus, in contrast to circumcision or uncircumcision, which are nothing. Those who walk by this rule are blessed with peace and mercy.

l: sowing and reaping, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
s: Sowing and reaping is a principle that whatever a man sows he reaps, so God is not mocked. Sowing to the flesh yields corruption, sowing to the Spirit yields eternal life; believers will reap in due season if they persist in doing good.

This document is a five-chapter letter from Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy to the assembly of the Thessalonians, a young community of believers. It combines thanksgiving, personal recollection, pastoral exhortation, and teaching about the Lord's return. Chapter 1 opens with greeting and thanks to God for the Thessalonians' work of faith, labor of love, and perseverance of hope. The Good News came to them in power and the Holy Spirit. They imitated the writers and the Lord, received the word amid affliction with joy, and became an example across Macedonia and Achaia. Others report how they turned from idols to serve a living God and await his Son Jesus from heaven. Chapter 2 recalls the writers' visit. Despite suffering at Philippi, they spoke boldly and without flattery, greed, or desire for glory. They were gentle like a nursing mother and exhorting like a father, and they worked night and day to avoid burdening anyone. The believers accepted the message as God's word and suffered from their own countrymen, as the assemblies in Judea did. The writers longed to see them again, but Satan hindered them. They call the believers their hope, joy, and crown. Chapter 3 explains that, unable to bear the separation, the writers stayed in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen and comfort the believers, fearing the tempter had undone their labor. Timothy returned with good news of the believers' faith and love, which comforted the writers. They give thanks, pray night and day to see them, and ask that the Lord make the believers increase in love and be blameless in holiness at Jesus' coming. Chapter 4 exhorts the believers to please God and be sanctified: avoid sexual immorality, control their bodies honorably, not wrong a brother or sister, grow in brotherly love, live quietly, and work with their own hands. It then addresses those who have fallen asleep: believers should not grieve without hope. The Lord will descend with a shout and God's trumpet, the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord. They are to comfort one another with these words. Chapter 5 says the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, bringing sudden destruction on those saying "Peace and safety." The believers, children of light, are to stay awake and sober, wearing faith, love, and the hope of salvation. God appointed them to salvation through Christ, who died so they may live with him. A series of exhortations follows: respect leaders, be at peace, support the weak, rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks, and test all things. The letter closes with a prayer for complete sanctification, a request for prayer, greetings, a command to read it to all, and a blessing of grace.

Paul is the apostle who, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to the assembly of the Thessalonians. The records present him as entrusted with the Good News of God, which he preached to them, seeking to please God rather than men. Though he suffered shamefully at Philippi and could have claimed apostolic authority, he was gentle like a nursing mother, exhorted them as a father would, and worked night and day so as not to burden anyone. The letter opens with greetings, thanks and prayer, and recalls how the group behaved among the believers. It then tells of Satan hindering their attempts to visit. Unable to bear separation, they stayed at Athens and sent Timothy to learn of the believers' faith. His good report comforted them, and they rejoice, give thanks, and pray night and day to see the Thessalonians and perfect what is lacking in their faith.

Timothy is the authors' brother and God's servant in the Good News of Christ. He was sent to establish and comfort the Thessalonians about their faith, then returned with glad news of their faith, love, and longing to see the authors.

The assembly of the Thessalonians is a community of believers addressed as standing in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, loved and chosen by God. It is remembered by Paul, Silvanus and Timothy for its work of faith, labor of love and perseverance of hope. Its most important features are its conversion and endurance: it turned from idols to serve a living and true God, waits for his Son from heaven, and is appointed to salvation rather than wrath. It received the word amid affliction with the joy of the Holy Spirit, imitated Paul and the Lord, and became an example to believers in Macedonia and Achaia. The records unfold through the letter's chapters. Chapter 1 recalls its faith, imitation and turning to God. Chapter 2 shows it receiving the message as God's word, suffering as the assemblies in Judea did, and being called the authors' hope, joy and crown at the Lord's coming. Chapter 3 tells of Timothy being sent to establish and comfort it, its steadfastness, its good memories of the authors and longing to see them, and prayer that its love would abound. Chapter 4 exhorts it to please God, live in sanctification, lead a quiet life, and praises its love for all the brothers in Macedonia; it is told to comfort one another about those who have fallen asleep and about the Lord's coming. Chapter 5 calls it children of light and of the day, not of darkness, urges watchfulness, faith, love and hope of salvation, respect for leaders and peace, and closes with requests for prayer, greetings and that the letter be read to all the holy brothers.

God, called "our God and Father," is the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ and the one in whom the Thessalonian assembly exists, source of grace and peace. The records present him as a living and true God who raised his Son from the dead. At the outset he is thanked in prayer, and the believers turned to serve him. He approved the writers, entrusted them with the Good News, and tests hearts and witnesses motives. He calls believers into his own Kingdom and glory, and his word works in them. His declared will is their sanctification: he called them to holiness, not uncleanness, and gave them his Holy Spirit and taught them to love. He will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus. He did not appoint them to wrath but to salvation through Jesus Christ. Called the God of peace, he is asked to sanctify them completely, and he is faithful: the one who calls will also do it. Giving thanks in everything is his will.

Lord Jesus Christ is God's Son, named with God the Father as the one in whom the assembly exists and a source of grace and peace. Certain Jews killed him, yet God raised him from the dead; he died and rose again, which grounds believers' hope, and he died for them so they may live together with him whether they wake or sleep. The Thessalonians imitated him and await him from heaven, and he delivers them from the wrath to come. He is also an avenger in matters of sexual immorality and wronging others. The records look ahead to his coming: he will descend from heaven with a shout, the archangel's voice and God's trumpet, come with all his saints, and be with believers forever. At that coming their hearts, spirit, soul and body are to be kept blameless in holiness. The letter closes with a blessing of his grace.

The Good News of God is a message that came to the Thessalonians not in word only but in power, the Holy Spirit, and much assurance. Those entrusted with it told it boldly amid conflict, free of burden, imparting their own souls, though opponents forbade speaking to the Gentiles. The Thessalonians received it joyfully in affliction, and the word spread through Macedonia, Achaia, and everywhere.

l: afflictions (suffering of the believers and authors), 1 Thessalonians
s: The authors say they were appointed to affliction and told the Thessalonians beforehand that they would suffer it, as indeed happened. Timothy was sent so that no one would be moved by these afflictions. The authors were comforted in their own distress and affliction through the believers' faith.

The Jews are portrayed as a group who killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, displeased God, and opposed all men. They forbid speaking to Gentiles so Gentiles may be saved, thereby filling up their sins, until wrath comes upon them fully.

lacks something to be perfected [authors pray to perfect it] Timothy was sent to establish and comfort the Thessalonians concerning their faith, and the authors feared the tempter might have undone it. Timothy's report of their faith brought the authors comfort in their affliction, and they say they live if the believers stand fast in the Lord. The authors pray night and day to perfect what is lacking in it.

l: the Lord's coming and the resurrection of the dead, 1 Thessalonians
s: involves Lord Jesus [descends from heaven with a shout, archangel's voice and God's trumpet] The Lord will descend from heaven with a shout, the voice of the archangel and God's trumpet, and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then the living believers will be caught up with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and this teaching is given so the believers will not grieve without hope and will comfort one another.

l: those who have fallen asleep (the dead in Christ), 1 Thessalonians
s: Those who have fallen asleep in Jesus, the dead in Christ, will be brought by God with him and rise first at the Lord's coming, before the living.

l: the living believers at the Lord's coming, 1 Thessalonians
s: The living believers left until the Lord's coming will not precede the dead in Christ. The dead rise first, then the living are caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and all are with the Lord forever.

is will of God Sanctification is stated to be God's will, including abstaining from sexual immorality and each person controlling his own body in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who don't know God. No one should take advantage of or wrong a brother or sister in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger, and whoever rejects this rejects God, who gave his Holy Spirit.

needs_no_writing brothers (the Thessalonian believers) [they are taught by God] The writers say the believers need no one to write to them about brotherly love, because they are taught by God to love one another. They already show it toward all the brothers in Macedonia, yet are exhorted to abound in it more and more.

comes_like thief in the night [manner of arrival] The day of the Lord is said to come like a thief in the night, something the recipients already know well. It brings sudden destruction, like birth pains on a pregnant woman, on those who say "Peace and safety," but it should not overtake the brothers, who are not in darkness.

l: those who say peace and safety, 1 Thessalonians
s: A group proclaiming "Peace and safety" is suddenly overtaken by destruction like birth pains on a pregnant woman; they will in no way escape, and are linked to those sleeping and drunk in the night.

A collection of Christian ethical exhortations. Early items stress rejoicing always, praying without ceasing, giving thanks in everything, testing all things, holding to the good, abstaining from evil, and not returning evil for evil. The Chapter 5 summary expands them: build each other up, honor leaders, be at peace, admonish the disorderly, support the weak, be patient, and not quench the Spirit.

l: Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians
s: This is Paul's Second Letter to the Thessalonians, a three-chapter letter sent by Paul with Silvanus and Timothy to the assembly of the Thessalonians. It first encourages the community, then corrects a misunderstanding about the Lord's coming, and finally gives practical instructions about conduct. In Chapter 1, Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians' growing faith and love and praises their perseverance through persecution. He says God will repay those who afflict them and give relief to the afflicted when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven, while those who do not know God or obey the Good News face eternal destruction. He prays that God will count them worthy of their calling. Chapter 2 urges them not to be shaken by claims that the day of Christ has already come. That day will not arrive until the rebellion occurs and the man of sin, the son of destruction, is revealed, exalting himself as God and working through Satan with lying wonders. Those who refused the truth are deceived and judged. The writer thanks God for choosing them for salvation, tells them to stand firm in the traditions they were taught, and asks that they be comforted and established. In Chapter 3, Paul requests prayer for the word to spread and for deliverance from evil men. He commands the brothers to withdraw from those who walk in rebellion, points to his own example of working night and day, and repeats that anyone unwilling to work should not eat. He tells idle busybodies to work quietly, urges the brothers not to grow weary in doing right, and closes with a personal greeting and a blessing of peace and grace.

l: Paul, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians
s: Paul is a letter-writing apostle who, together with Silvanus and Timothy, addresses the Thessalonian assembly. He opens by thanking God for them, boasting of their perseverance and faith, and praying always that they be counted worthy of their calling. He closes by requesting prayer for the word's spread and deliverance from evil men, commanding withdrawal from the rebellious, and offering his own labor as a model to imitate, though he had a right to support. He authenticates each letter with his own handwriting.

l: assembly of the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians
s: The assembly of the Thessalonians is a community of believers addressed as being in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, loved by the Lord, chosen by God for salvation, and called through the Good News to obtain Christ's glory. Its faith and love are praised, and it endures persecutions and afflictions with perseverance, suffering for God's Kingdom and promised relief when Jesus is revealed. It is then urged not to be shaken by claims that the day of Christ has come, to stand firm in the traditions taught, and finally to pray for Paul, imitate his work, withdraw from rebellious brothers, not grow weary in doing right, and admonish the disobedient as a brother.

l: God, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians
s: God, called our Father, is the divine figure in Paul's Second Letter to the Thessalonians. He is thanked as the source of grace and peace with the Lord Jesus Christ. His righteous judgment appears in the Thessalonians' suffering: he will repay affliction to their afflicters and give relief to the afflicted when the Lord Jesus is revealed. He sends a powerful delusion on those who rejected the love of the truth. He chose and called the brothers for salvation, loved them, and gave eternal comfort and good hope through grace.

l: Lord Jesus Christ, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians
s: The Lord Jesus Christ appears across the three chapters of Paul's Second Letter to the Thessalonians as Lord, named with God the Father as a source of grace and peace. In chapter 1 he will be revealed from heaven with mighty angels in flaming fire, punish those who don't know God, and be glorified in his saints and admired among believers. Chapter 2 centers on his coming and the gathering of believers; he will kill the lawless one with the breath of his mouth, and believers are called to obtain his glory. Chapter 3 presents him as faithful, guarding from the evil one, and the Lord of peace, closing with a blessing of grace.

l: those who afflict the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians
s: These people afflict the Thessalonian believers. It is called a righteous thing with God to repay affliction to them.

l: those who don't know God or obey the Good News, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians

Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, writes with Timothy to Philemon, to Apphia, to Archippus, and to the assembly in Philemon's house, greeting them and thanking God for Philemon's love and faith. Paul says he could command Philemon but instead appeals out of love on behalf of Onesimus, whom he became father to in his chains. He is sending Onesimus back, asking Philemon to receive him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, and offers to repay anything Onesimus owes. Paul expresses confidence in Philemon's obedience, asks him to prepare a guest room in hope of being restored to him through prayer, and relays greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke before closing with a blessing.

Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, writes with Timothy to Philemon and the assembly in his house. He appeals rather than commands on behalf of Onesimus, sends him back, and promises in his own hand to repay anything Onesimus owes. He asks Philemon to prepare a guest room, hoping to be restored to him through prayer.

Philemon is addressed as Paul's beloved fellow worker, praised for his love and faith toward the Lord Jesus and all the saints, and for refreshing the hearts of the saints. Paul appeals to him to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother rather than a slave, and to put any wrong or debt to Paul's account. Paul says Philemon owes him even his own self and expresses confidence that he will do even more than asked.

Onesimus is called Paul's child, whom Paul became father to in his chains. He was once useless to Philemon but is now useful to both Paul and Philemon, and Paul sends him back, describing him as his own heart. Paul asks that Philemon receive him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, in the flesh and in the Lord.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to Philemon
s: Jesus Christ is named as the Lord, in whom Paul is a prisoner and from whom, with God the Father, grace and peace come. Philemon's faith is directed toward him, and the knowledge of every good thing is said to be in Christ Jesus. Paul grounds his boldness and his hope for refreshment in him, and closes by wishing his grace be with Philemon's spirit.

This document is the Letter from James, a five-chapter exhortation written by James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion. Its central concern is that faith must show itself in conduct, and the people who matter most are the scattered believers addressed as brothers, set against the rich, the proud, and those who misuse speech or favor the wealthy. Chapter 1 opens by urging readers to count trials as joy because testing produces endurance, to ask God for wisdom without doubting, and to recognize that temptation comes from one's own lust, not from God, while every good gift comes from the Father of lights. It ends by calling them to be swift to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger, doers of the word and not only hearers, and to practice pure religion by visiting orphans and widows and staying unstained by the world. Chapter 2 forbids partiality, illustrated by the man in a gold ring favored over the poor man, and says partiality breaks the royal law to love one's neighbor. It then argues that faith without works is dead, citing the believing demons, Abraham, and Rahab, and concludes that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Chapter 3 warns against becoming teachers too readily and turns to the tongue, small like a bit or rudder yet able to set a forest ablaze, untameable, and wrong when it both blesses God and curses people. It contrasts earthly wisdom of jealousy and ambition with wisdom from above, pure, peaceable, and merciful. Chapter 4 traces quarrels to pleasures and lusts, calls friendship with the world hostility toward God, and commands submission to God, resisting the devil, drawing near to God, and humbling oneself. It forbids judging a brother and rebukes confident business planning, reminding readers life is a vapor and they should say 'If the Lord wills.' Chapter 5 warns the rich that their corroded wealth and withheld wages will testify against them, then urges patience until the Lord's coming, citing the farmer, the prophets, and Job. It forbids oaths and closes with prayer: for the suffering, for the sick anointed by elders, for mutual confession, with Elijah as an example and the hope of turning back a wandering sinner.

James, a servant of God and the Lord Jesus Christ, writes a letter to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion, exhorting them on trials, wisdom, temptation, listening, and doing the word, and defining pure religion.

God, as presented in the Letter from James, is the one, unchanging Father of lights, source of every good and perfect gift. He cannot be tempted by evil and tempts no one. He gives wisdom liberally and without reproach to those who ask in faith, and by his own will gave birth to believers by the word of truth. He chose the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the promised Kingdom, and promises the crown of life to those who love him. Abraham believed him and was called his friend; even the demons believe he is one. People are made in his image, though the tongue both blesses him and curses them. A friend of the world becomes his enemy. He resists the proud, gives grace to the humble, draws near to those who draw near, and exalts the humble. As the only lawgiver, he is able to save and to destroy. Called Lord of Armies, he hears the cries of the defrauded reapers. His coming is at hand, the judge stands at the door, and he is full of compassion and mercy, as seen in Job.

l: twelve tribes in the Dispersion, The Letter from James
s: The twelve tribes in the Dispersion are the addressees of a letter greeted by James. Called brothers and given an honorable name, they are oppressed by the rich, who drag them before the courts, and they will be judged by the law of freedom; teachers among them face heavier judgment. The letter opens by urging them to count trials as joy, ask God for wisdom, resist temptation, and be doers of the word. It then warns against partiality and dishonoring the poor, and calls for mercy and works along with faith. It cautions about teaching and the tongue, and urges gentle, wise conduct over jealousy and selfish ambition. It then rebukes fighting, coveting, and double-mindedness, calls them adulterers and enemies of God if they befriend the world, and tells them to submit to God, resist the devil, draw near, and humble themselves. It closes by commanding patience until the Lord's coming, avoiding oaths, praying, confessing sins to one another, and turning back any who wander from the truth.
